query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: In multi‐element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, the preservation of structural and chemical stability under high‐temperature catalytic and thermoelectric service conditions is governed by the balance between high configurational entropy (which stabilizes the single-phase solid solution) and the enhanced surface-driven atomic diffusion and segregation (which promote phase decomposition).
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles with a random, near-equiatomic solid-solution structure (i.e., an HEA-like phase) synthesized by physical and/or chemical fabrication methods with minimal size dispersion and no pre-existing phase separation.
generation.intervention: Prepare size-selected (or surface-modified) nanoparticle batches that vary primarily in their average particle size (and hence surface-to-volume ratio) while keeping the composition constant, and then expose them to controlled thermal treatments across the catalytic (773–1173 K) or thermoelectric (473–1923 K) regimes.
generation.conditions: Isothermal aging/exposure under inert or reactive atmospheres at targeted service temperatures (e.g., 1173 K for catalysis and up to 1923 K for thermoelectric applications) for durations representative of service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The interplay between the bulk configurational entropy that favors a homogeneous solid-solution phase and the nanoparticle surface energy that accelerates atomic diffusion and promotes elemental segregation or secondary phase formation at surfaces or interfaces.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy in near-equiatomic systems thermodynamically stabilizes the single-phase solid solution. However, in nanoscale particles, the high surface-to-volume ratio elevates surface energy contributions. At elevated temperatures, thermally activated diffusion at the surface accelerates elemental segregation or the nucleation of secondary (ordered or intermetallic) phases, undermining the stability established by bulk entropy. Thus, nanoparticles with higher relative surface area (i.e. smaller sizes) are expected to show a higher propensity for structural and chemical instability while larger nanoparticles should maintain their single-phase structure longer under the same conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline (standard nanoparticle size distribution), nanoparticles with a reduced surface-to-volume ratio (i.e. larger sizes or with surface-passivating modifications) will exhibit improved retention of the single-phase solid solution structure and homogeneous elemental distribution after thermal exposure. Conversely, smaller nanoparticles will show early signs of phase decomposition or surface segregation (e.g., detectable by new diffraction peaks or compositional gradients) under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles produced under standard synthesis conditions, exhibiting moderate size distribution, which may show some degradation at the highest service temperatures.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to near-equiatomic, single-phase nanoparticles in temperature regimes relevant to catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) operations. It may not hold for materials with significant pre-existing phase segregation, non-equiatomic compositions, or when extrinsic stabilizing mechanisms (e.g., strong capping layers or oxide shells) dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical nanoparticle size (or surface energy threshold) at which surface-driven diffusion overtakes entropy stabilization is not well established, nor is the quantitative dependence on the specific alloying elements, making the effect size and temperature threshold somewhat uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of the same near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles that differ primarily in their average particle size (e.g., one set with an average diameter of ~10 nm and another with ~30 nm) while keeping the composition constant. Subject both batches to identical isothermal annealing treatments at a service-relevant temperature (e.g., 1173 K for catalytic conditions) for an extended duration. Optionally, include a surface-passivated variant to further isolate surface-energy effects.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to detect the emergence of secondary phases or changes in lattice parameters
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with energy dispersed spectroscopy (EDS) mapping to assess elemental distribution and surface segregation
Surface-sensitive techniques (e.g., X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, XPS) to quantify surface composition changes
Performance tests such as catalytic activity measurements before and after thermal treatment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the small and large nanoparticles (or the passivated and unpassivated versions) exhibit statistically equivalent phase stability and elemental homogeneity under the identical thermal treatment, then the hypothesis that the balance between configurational entropy and surface-driven diffusion governs the observed stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys (HEAs), complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), and multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are the most common names of a new group of materials [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ] introduced by Yeh et al. [ [6] ] and Cantor et al. [ [7] ] in the beginning of this century. Many definitions were proposed for such materials, but in general they consist of multiple (usually at least five) elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition [ [2] ]. This approach is different from the traditional alloy design using one (or maximum two) principal element and other minor elements. The presence of many elements in equiatomic (or near) composition leads to high mixing entropy and thus to many interesting properties [ [2] , [5] ]. One of such effects is the existence of a random solid solution and simple body centered cubic (bcc) or faced centered cubic (fcc) structure. Recently HEAs with hexagonal closed packed (hcp) structure have been reported as well [ [8] , [9] ]. A new approach to HEA design using the valence electron concentration (VEC) was recently proposed with the aim of increasing the plasticity of these alloys [ [10] , [11] ]. Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.
